extracted.intended_audience: journalists, journalism students, media scholars, and readers interested in media ethics
extracted.subtask_description: A feature-length case study of the Janet Cooke fabrication that outlines changes to newsroom practice and the ethical standards journalists and editors are held to. Useful for examining newsroom accountability, source management, and hiring/vetting reforms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prohibition on fabrication
rubrics_metrics.description: Fabricating quotes, characters, or entire stories is an unacceptable transgression against journalistic truth (exemplified by Janet Cooke's invention of 'Jimmy' and later cases such as Stephen Glass and Jayson Blair).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Fabrication destroys institutional trust and carries severe consequences: public disgrace, returned awards (the Post returned the Pulitzer), and long-term reputational damage. Avoid literary license that invents essential facts or people.

rubrics_metrics.name: Editors' responsibility to question reporters' stories
rubrics_metrics.description: Editors must actively question and probe reporters' work rather than simply trusting them—raising the question: should writers be considered 'guilty until proven accurate'?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Cooke case shows editors interrogating and pressuring the reporter, conducting investigations, and demanding explanations. Strong editorial skepticism and oversight are necessary safeguards against fraud.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reporters' duty to fact-check their own stories
rubrics_metrics.description: Writers are responsible for verifying the facts in their work and for not taking liberties in pursuit of more literary or compelling narratives.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Journalists should corroborate key details, verify identities and backgrounds, and avoid relying on unverifiable anecdotes or invented scenes. Failure to self-check can lead to career-ending scandals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hiring and résumé vetting practices
rubrics_metrics.description: News organizations must carefully review applicants' résumés and credentials (e.g., verifying degrees and claims) as part of responsible hiring.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: After Cooke, papers 'changed the way we hired people' and became 'much more careful about reviewing what they said in their résumé.' Implement background checks and confirm educational and employment claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Management and disclosure of unnamed sources
rubrics_metrics.description: Reporters should share the identities of unnamed sources with editors even if those sources remain unnamed publicly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Following Cooke, many outlets instituted policies requiring reporters to reveal unnamed-source identities to editors; memos from papers (including USA Today) formalized this practice and it 'remains an industry standard.' This balances source protection with editorial accountability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Transparency to readers (source citations and editors' notes)
rubrics_metrics.description: For investigative or literary pieces, newsrooms should be open with readers—providing source citations and explanatory editors' notes where appropriate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Publishers increased column space for citations and editors' notes after the scandal. Greater transparency helps restore and maintain public trust, especially for controversial stories.

rubrics_metrics.name: Institutional accountability and corrective action
rubrics_metrics.description: When journalistic failures occur, institutions must investigate, correct the record, and take concrete remedial actions (e.g., returning awards, reassignments, public explanations).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Post's ombudsman investigation, the return of Cooke's Pulitzer, and re-awarding the prize demonstrate forms of accountability. Prompt, public corrective measures help address trust breaches.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ombudsman / reader-liaison function
rubrics_metrics.description: An ombudsman serves as an internal moral compass and advocate for readers, helping to investigate failures and ease trust issues between the newsroom and the community.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cooke's exposure helped spark the rise of ombudsmen; their dual mission is to represent readers' interests and hold the newsroom accountable. Consider establishing or strengthening this role.

rubrics_metrics.name: Standardization and procedural safeguards in newsrooms
rubrics_metrics.description: Newsrooms should adopt standardized procedures and rules (less romanticized 'rogue' reporting) to reduce risk and ensure consistent ethical practice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Post-Cooke journalism became 'more homogenized and standardized, more corporate, more rule-driven.' While this may reduce certain freedoms, procedural safeguards (clear policies, documented approvals) protect integrity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limits on literary nonfiction's license
rubrics_metrics.description: Writers working in literary or creative nonfiction must not use artistic license to invent essential facts or people; factual accuracy remains paramount.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The story highlights 'the tendency of some writers, operating in the genre known as creative nonfiction, to take license' and warns of its perils. Maintain clear boundaries between dramatization and factual reporting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Community relations and sensitivity to affected communities
rubrics_metrics.description: News organizations should be mindful of how reporting affects communities—particularly marginalized groups—and work to maintain constructive community relations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cooke's piece provoked community outrage, especially among Black residents; post-scandal efforts increased emphasis on community relations. Avoid reporting that sensationalizes or harms communities without accountable justification and outreach.

rubrics_metrics.name: Awareness of diversity-hiring consequences and extra scrutiny dynamics
rubrics_metrics.description: Efforts to diversify newsrooms require careful handling so that beneficiaries are not unfairly stigmatized or placed under disproportionate scrutiny following ethical failures.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Cooke affair had collateral effects on perceptions of African-American journalists. Organizations should balance affirmative hiring with fair vetting and support, recognizing the potential for disproportionate fallout.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consideration of individual suitability and support for assignments
rubrics_metrics.description: Editors should assess whether individuals are psychologically and professionally equipped for high-pressure assignments and provide appropriate support.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Walt Harrington's view: 'any system should be thoughtful about that kind of person'—avoid pushing 'a flawed person into [something they couldn't handle].' Provide mentoring, oversight, and limits when needed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Maintain editorial audit trails and documentation
rubrics_metrics.description: Retain edit trails, draft histories, and records of editorial interactions to enable investigation and attribution if questions arise.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In the Cooke case an 'edit trail' flagged potential collaboration; such records can help reconstruct decision-making and detect inconsistencies during post-publication inquiries.

rubrics_metrics.name: Accurate award submission and category selection
rubrics_metrics.description: Entries for prizes must accurately represent the work and be submitted in the appropriate category; manipulation to secure awards undermines trust.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Pulitzer committee moved Cooke's entry from local news to feature-writing to favor an award—such practices raise concerns. Ensure transparent and appropriate submission processes.
